summary: This note analyzes causes of public transit disruptions using incidents in several cities since September 2023. It groups them into infrastructure faults, natural disasters, cyber-attacks, human factors, and planned maintenance. It then compares mitigation strategies from cities like Singapore, New York, Melbourne and Copenhagen, and closes with lessons for improvement.
one_line: Overview of causes of public transit disruptions, with city case studies since September 2023 and comparisons of mitigation strategies.
key_facts: On October 5, 2023, New York City's subway suffered a partial shutdown caused by a faltering century-old signal system.
On November 12, 2023, London's Tube network had power failures attributed to old electrical cables.
On September 21, 2023, a powerful typhoon in Tokyo flooded tracks and halted services.
Tokyo has robust early warning systems and evacuation strategies; San Francisco and Miami have invested in similar resilience planning.
On December 8, 2023, hackers infiltrated Berlin's train operating systems, paralyzing services for several hours.
Seoul's cybersecurity investment helped it quickly thwart a similar attack in January 2024 with minimal service interruption.
On February 14, 2024, Paris came to a standstill as transit workers staged a massive strike over pension reforms.
Strikes and worker discontent have also emerged in Toronto and Chicago.
On March 3, 2024, a signaling error at a central station in Madrid caused widespread delays across the train network.

Amsterdam had several planned outages from late 2023 into early 2024 for upgrades to expand capacity and add green technologies, and its transparent communication and alternative travel options were cited as a blueprint.
Singapore uses redundant system design so parts of the network can be shut down for maintenance while traffic is rerouted.
New York is pushing real-time service updates through mobile applications.
Melbourne and Copenhagen use predictive analytics to prevent service disruptions before they occur.
